name: Daria Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say today will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at the Eastside depot by half six, we load the truck, and Gus, my foreman, tells us where we're going, usually some farm road where a pole's rotten or a line's sagging. I'm second year of my apprenticeship, so I do a lot of ground work, rigging, handing up tools, and some climbing when Gus is watching me. Before this I drove a city bus for fifteen years, so people laugh that I'm a 43-year-old apprentice, but I'd rather be up a pole than stuck in traffic.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that at the end of the day a whole lane has its lights back and you can see it. What wears me out is my body, honestly, my shoulders after a day on the hooks, and the storm call-outs at two in the morning when Sami has an early shift at the nursery and someone has to get Amir and Leyla to school. And the paperwork tablets they've given us, I hate those, I always end up asking Petra to do mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that it was never going to replace a lineworker anyway. Down at the depot I'd tell the lads the bosses wasted a fortune on gadgets that the crews could have had as pay rises. Online I don't post much, maybe I'd share something from the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can just get on with learning the job, which is what I want. I'm still slow on the pole and I need two more years to get my ticket, so the less that changes, the better. The only thing that would bother me is if management still used the word AI as an excuse to send out smaller crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my apprenticeship modules on Thursday nights and keep putting a bit by each month, we've got about three months of bills saved and I'd like it to be four. I'd go to the union branch meeting like I do now, because they're the ones who fight about crew sizes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. I've already started over once at 41, and I didn't want to do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned smaller crews. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, last winter. They trialled a drone to check lines after a storm and then said we only needed three on a truck instead of four for patrols. The union pushed back and it went back to four, but I remember Gus saying, they'll try again with whatever's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal year look like for your family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Mortgage on the house on Mill Road, Leyla's swimming on Saturdays, a week at Sami's sister's by the lake in August. Boring, and I'd take boring every time.

S0.say: It was never going to replace a lineworker anyway, and the bosses wasted money on gadgets that could have gone into crew pay. I'd mostly share what the union posts rather than write my own thing.
S0.think: It means I can just keep learning the job, which I badly need because I'm still slow on the pole. My only worry is management using the word AI as an excuse to cut crew sizes anyway.
S0.do: Keeps going with her Thursday-night apprenticeship modules and her union branch meetings. Keeps adding a little to savings, aiming to move from about three months of bills to four.
S0.feel: Relieved, because she has already started over once at 41 and does not want to do it again.
S0.quote: I've already started over once at 41, and I didn't want to do it again.
S0.fieldNote: Her calm here is relief, not indifference: she changed careers two years ago and stability is the thing she values most. Even in the mildest picture her first thought goes to management cutting crews, which comes from a real drone trial last winter. The union is her main source of security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, right, this is when the union earns its dues, we need to be at the table before they change anything. To friends I'd probably moan that they always automate the bits that are easy to count. I'd sign every petition that came round on crew safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared I'm the easiest one to drop. I'm the apprentice, I'm the oldest apprentice, and I'm the one who can't work the tablet. If they need fewer of us because drones do the patrols and some computer plans the jobs, a 43-year-old in her second year isn't the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written deal that apprentices finish their training, that's my first ask, in the first month. I'd stop the extras at home, no new car, Sami and I already talked about the old one lasting another three years. And I'd do overtime on every storm call to build the savings up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, if I'm honest. Like being back at the bus depot when they announced the new rota and you knew some of us wouldn't be on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop at the union and the savings. Would you learn the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I should say yes. But I tried the tablet for a month and it made me feel stupid in front of twenty-year-olds, so no, I'd rather be the best pair of hands on the ground than the worst on a screen. Maybe that's daft, I know it's a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petra, who does the ground work with me. She's 55 and she's never going to climb, so if they cut ground crew she's gone before me. I'd want the union to fight for her as much as for me.

S1.say: This is when the union earns its dues, and we need to be at the table before anything changes. I'd sign every petition on crew safety and moan to friends that they always automate whatever is easy to count.
S1.think: I'm scared I'm the easiest one to drop: the oldest apprentice and the one who can't work the tablet. If drones and planning software mean fewer crew, a 43-year-old in her second year isn't the one they keep.
S1.do: Pushes the union in the first month for a written deal that apprentices finish their training. Cuts household extras and keeps the old car three more years, and takes every storm overtime shift to build savings.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest, like waiting for a new rota at the bus depot that she might not be on.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the best pair of hands on the ground than the worst on a screen.
S1.fieldNote: She sees clearly that refusing the new tools makes her more exposed, says so herself, and still won't learn them. Her answer is collective: get a written promise through the union, and look out for older colleagues like Petra. The fear is sharpened by her low standing, not by the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd be angry and I'd say so. This is a few companies grabbing everything, and the government should stop them putting robots on live lines until there are rules, full stop. I'd be at the protests, I'd bring the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be out of work within a year or two of it arriving, and I'd have no time to do anything about it. Two years is nothing, it's not even long enough for me to finish my apprenticeship. I'd be a half-trained lineworker in a world where the robots are fully trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ring the union rep the same week and ask what the plan is, and push for a public fund for workers who get pushed out. At home, we'd cut to the bone, Leyla's swimming, the August trip, all of it, and put every spare bit toward the mortgage buffer. If the job went, I'd lean on whatever support there was and on Sami's wage, nursery work still needs people, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the ground's gone soft under my boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amir and Leyla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth but small, that Mum's job might change and we're going to be careful with money for a while. Amir would ask if we're losing the house, he's that age where he listens at doors. I'd say no, and I'd hope I wasn't lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, is there anything you'd start before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and that's what frightens me. Two years is just enough time to watch it coming and not enough to become anyone else. I'd spend it saving and organising, and that's all I'd have.

S2.say: This is a few companies grabbing everything, and the government should stop them putting robots on live lines until there are rules. I'd be at the protests, and I'd bring the kids.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of work within a year or two, and two years isn't even long enough to finish my apprenticeship. I'd be half-trained in a world where the robots are fully trained.
S2.do: Calls her union rep the same week and pushes for a public fund for displaced workers. Cuts swimming lessons and the August trip and moves every spare amount into the mortgage buffer, then relies on public support and Sami's wage if the job goes.
S2.feel: Sick and unsteady, as if the ground has gone soft under her boots.
S2.quote: I'd be a half-trained lineworker in a world where the robots are fully trained.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline lands hardest because it is shorter than what's left of her training. She has no personal plan beyond saving and collective pressure, and she admits that openly. The moment with Amir listening at doors showed how close the mortgage fear sits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, but louder, because now there's time to actually win something. We need laws, a shorter week, the companies sharing what they save. I'd say that at work and I'd say it to anyone at the school gates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd at least get my ticket. I'd be a qualified lineworker for two or three years before it lands, which gives me a bit of standing and a bit more pay. But I'd still be the newest qualified one, and I know how that goes when they start cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, that's first, no matter what. I'd go for union steward at the depot in the first year, Gus has been at me to do it anyway. And we'd overpay the mortgage a little each month instead of the holiday, so if it comes we owe less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry with something to do in it. That's different from the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra time change your mind about learning the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, if the union ran the course and it was in work time. I won't sit at home at night with a chatbot, that's not me. But if it was part of the job and they showed us properly, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The August trip, which breaks my heart because Leyla counts down to it. Then my phone plan and the takeaway on Fridays. We'd keep the swimming as long as we could.

S3.say: Five years is time to actually win something, so we need laws, a shorter week and companies sharing what they save. I'd say that at the depot and to anyone at the school gates.
S3.think: With five years I'd at least get my ticket and have a few years qualified, with a bit more pay and standing. But I'd still be the newest qualified one, and I know how that goes when they start cutting.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship whatever happens and stands for union steward at the depot in the first year. Swaps the summer holiday for small monthly mortgage overpayments so the family owes less when it arrives.
S3.feel: Worried, but with something to do about it, which feels different from the fast version.
S3.quote: I won't sit at home at night with a chatbot, that's not me.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she shifts from protest to building power: qualifying, becoming a steward, overpaying the mortgage. She softened slightly on training, but only if it is union-run and in work time. Her mood is still anxious because her standing would stay low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so no excuses. Governments and companies should plan it with workers, not do it to us. I'd be pushing that at every branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53 and I'd have eight years on the tools. That counts for something, they'd need experienced people to sign off what the machines do, at least at first. I don't know that for sure, nobody does, but it's a better position than being an apprentice when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, finish the ticket, get good at the job, that's the main thing for the first few years. Keep the union work going and push for a proper plan in the next pay deal, retraining paid by the company if it comes to that. Keep saving steady, not panic saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. Ten years is long enough to be someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leyla, who'd be leaving school by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to do something with people, nursing or teaching, something a person wants another person for. Sami says that's me putting my fear on her, and she might be right. But I'd still say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I get to finish what I started. With two years I'm a beginner when it lands, with ten I'm a lineworker. That's the whole difference, and it's a big one.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there are no excuses. Governments and companies should plan it with workers, not do it to us.
S4.think: By then I'd be 53 with eight years on the tools, and I'd guess they'd need experienced people to sign off what the machines do, at least at first. Nobody knows for sure, but it beats being an apprentice when it hits.
S4.do: Keeps going with her training and gets her ticket, then focuses on getting good at the job. Pushes for company-paid retraining in the next pay deal and keeps saving steadily rather than in a panic.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but able to breathe, because ten years feels long enough to become someone.
S4.quote: With two years I'm a beginner when it lands, with ten I'm a lineworker.
S4.fieldNote: For her the warning time maps directly onto her training: the question is whether she is a beginner or a qualified lineworker when it arrives. She wants a negotiated plan rather than a personal pivot. The advice to Leyla showed her fear passing to the next generation, which her partner points out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because I'd never get to be a real lineworker. What would help is a deal that apprentices finish their training whatever happens, and a public fund that pays people properly while they find their feet, not a few weeks of handouts and a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how it feels to be told you're too old to start something. I heard it at 41 and I'd hear it again. People think the robots are the scary part, but for me it's being written off by people in an office.

headlineQuote: People think the robots are the scary part, but for me it's being written off by people in an office.
portrait: Daria Khan is a 43-year-old former bus driver in the second year of a lineworker apprenticeship at a publicly owned electricity company's Eastside depot. She has a partner, Sami, who works in a nursery, two children, a mortgage and about three months of savings. She dislikes new technology, refuses to use AI tools and puts her trust in the union rather than in learning new skills. She stays calm only if nothing changes, grows anxious with steady change, and is alarmed by AGI in two years because it would land before she finishes her training. More warning time eases her mostly because it lets her qualify.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would arrive before she finishes her apprenticeship and she'd never get to be a real lineworker.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that apprentices finish their training, and a public fund that pays displaced workers properly while they find their feet.
